title: Why Every Growing Business Needs a Legal Retainer
excerpt: Most businesses call a lawyer when something has already gone wrong. A legal retainer turns that around, giving you a legal partner who knows your business before problems arise.
content:
Most businesses only call a lawyer when something has already gone wrong: a contract dispute, a demand letter, an employee claim or a deal that suddenly looks risky. By then, options have narrowed and the costs, in money and in time, are usually higher than they needed to be.

A legal retainer turns that pattern around. Instead of instructing an advocate only in a crisis, your business works with a legal partner on an ongoing basis. At Crest Advocates, we describe it simply: we don't just show up when things go wrong. On retainer, we become your legal partner.

What a legal retainer is

A retainer is an agreement between a business and a law firm for ongoing legal support. The scope is agreed at the start, so both sides know what is covered. Within that scope, the business can raise questions as they come up, have documents reviewed and get advice before decisions are made, rather than after.

The details vary from firm to firm and from business to business. A retainer for a young company that is signing its first supplier contracts will look different from one for an established business with a large team. What matters is that the arrangement fits how your business actually runs.

Why growth creates legal questions

As a business grows, the number of legal decisions it makes grows with it. New staff mean employment contracts and workplace policies. New customers and suppliers mean agreements, terms of trade and, occasionally, unpaid invoices. New premises mean leases. New partners or investors mean shareholder arrangements. Each of these is manageable on its own. Together, they can stretch a busy owner or management team thin.

Many businesses handle these questions as they arise, sometimes by reusing old templates or relying on what worked last time. That can be fine, until it isn't. A clause that made sense for one deal may not protect you in the next, and a policy written years ago may not reflect how your team works today.

What a retainer gives your business

A good retainer is about more than access to a lawyer. It is about having someone who already understands your business when you need advice. For our retainer clients, that means:

  • Fast responses when it matters. When a question comes up, you have a direct line to a team that already knows your business.
  • Advice that fits your business. Because we learn how you operate and what you are trying to achieve, our advice is shaped around your goals rather than offered in the abstract.
  • Fixed, predictable fees. You agree the arrangement in advance, which makes legal support easier to plan for.
  • Problems solved before they grow. Regular contact makes it easier to spot issues early, when they are simpler to deal with.

Signs your business may be ready

There is no single point at which a business needs a retainer, but some signs are common. You may be signing contracts regularly. You may have a growing team. You may find yourself holding back on decisions because you are unsure of the legal position, or paying for one-off advice on similar questions again and again. You may simply want the confidence of knowing that someone has your back.

The aim of a retainer is simple: to let you make decisions with confidence, knowing your legal position before you act.

Questions to ask before you sign up

Before entering any retainer, it is worth being clear on a few points. What exactly is included, and what would be treated as separate work? How do you contact the team, and who will you be dealing with? How are fees set, and when are they reviewed? How will the arrangement be adjusted as your business changes? A firm you can trust will welcome these questions and answer them plainly.

Starting the conversation

Every business is different, and the right retainer depends on your sector, your size and the kind of decisions you face. A good first step is a conversation about how your business works and where legal support would make the most difference.

title: 5 Things to Look for When Choosing an Advocate
excerpt: Choosing an advocate is an important decision. Here are five things worth checking, from a current practising certificate to how the advocate communicates and handles your information.
content:
Whether you are buying land, starting a business, dealing with a family matter or facing a dispute, the advocate you choose will shape how the process feels and how well you understand your options. It is a decision worth taking time over.

You need more than legal advice. You need someone who listens, understands your needs and stands by you when it matters most. Here are five things worth looking for.

1. A current practising certificate

In Kenya, an advocate must be admitted to the Roll of Advocates and must hold a current practising certificate to offer legal services. This is the most basic check, and it is also one of the most important. The Law Society of Kenya provides a way for the public to confirm whether an advocate is in good standing, and a reputable advocate will be comfortable with you checking.

Be cautious of anyone who offers legal services but is reluctant to confirm their status, or who asks you to pay for legal work through unofficial channels.

2. Someone who listens and communicates clearly

Good legal advice starts with understanding your situation properly. At your first meeting, notice whether the advocate asks questions, listens to the answers and takes the time to understand what matters to you, rather than jumping straight to conclusions.

Clear communication matters just as much. The law can be complex, but advice should not be confusing. You should come away understanding your options, the steps involved and what is expected of you. If you leave a meeting unsure what was said, it is fair to ask for it to be explained again in plain language.

  • Do they explain things without unnecessary jargon?
  • Do they tell you how and when they will update you?
  • Do they respond to your questions within a reasonable time?

3. Relevant experience

The law covers a wide range of areas, and many advocates focus on particular kinds of work. An advocate who regularly handles matters like yours will be familiar with the process, the documents involved and the issues that commonly arise.

It is reasonable to ask whether an advocate handles matters similar to yours and how they would approach your situation. The answer should be honest. If a matter falls outside an advocate's usual work, a good advocate will say so.

4. Transparency about fees and process

Uncertainty about cost is one of the most common worries people have about instructing a lawyer. A trustworthy advocate will discuss fees openly before work begins, explain how they are calculated and tell you about any other costs you may need to cover.

The same openness should apply to the process. You should understand what will happen, what you will need to provide and what decisions you may need to make along the way. Be wary of anyone who promises a particular outcome. No honest advocate can promise how a matter will end, but they can explain your options and the risks involved.

The right advocate will not tell you what you want to hear. They will tell you what you need to know, clearly and honestly.

5. Respect for confidentiality

When you speak to an advocate about a legal matter, you may need to share personal, financial or commercial information. You should feel confident that it will be handled with discretion.

Pay attention to how an advocate treats information from the start. Do they explain how your information will be used and stored? Do they ask you to discuss sensitive details in person or in a secure setting, rather than over an open message or web form? Small signs like these say a lot about how seriously a firm takes confidentiality.

Making your decision

Choosing an advocate is ultimately about trust. Credentials matter, but so does the feeling that you are being heard and that your interests are being taken seriously. Professionalism, integrity and a client-focused approach should be visible in every interaction, from the first phone call onwards.

title: What to Expect at Your First Legal Consultation
excerpt: A first meeting with an advocate can feel daunting. Knowing what to bring, what to ask and how confidentiality works will help you make the most of it.
content:
For many people, a first meeting with an advocate is an unfamiliar experience. You may be dealing with something stressful, and you may not be sure what to say, what to bring or what will happen next. A little preparation goes a long way, and it will help you get the most out of the time.

The purpose of a first consultation

A first consultation is a chance for the advocate to understand your situation and for you to understand your options. It is also an opportunity to decide whether you are comfortable working with that advocate.

In most cases, the advocate will want to hear what happened, what you are hoping to achieve and whether there are any urgent concerns. They may ask a number of questions to get a clear picture. By the end, you should have a better sense of where you stand and what the next steps could be.

What to bring

The more relevant information you bring, the more useful the conversation is likely to be. Depending on your matter, it may help to bring:

  • Your national ID or passport
  • Any agreements or contracts connected to the matter
  • Letters, emails or messages you have sent or received
  • Title documents, search results or other property records, for land matters
  • Court papers or official notices, if you have received any
  • A short written timeline of the key events and dates
  • A list of the questions you want to ask

Do not worry if you do not have everything. Bring what you can, and the advocate will tell you if anything else is needed.

Questions you might ask

A consultation is a two-way conversation. It is your opportunity to understand the process as well as the law. You might ask:

  • What are my options, and what are the advantages and disadvantages of each?
  • What will the process involve, and what will you need from me?
  • How are your fees calculated, and are there other costs I should expect?
  • Who will be handling my matter, and how will you keep me updated?
  • Is there anything I should do, or avoid doing, in the meantime?

It is perfectly reasonable to write the answers down, or to ask for anything important to be confirmed in writing.

Confidentiality

People are often unsure how much to share at a first meeting. It is important to be open with your advocate, because advice is only as good as the information it is based on. Advocates are bound by professional duties of confidentiality, and a good firm treats what you share with care.

That said, the way you share information matters. Web forms and open messages are fine for arranging a meeting, but they are not the right place for sensitive details. Keep the specifics for the consultation itself.

Be honest and complete with your advocate. The details you are least comfortable sharing are often the ones that matter most.

What happens afterwards

After a first consultation, you may receive a summary of the advice, an outline of the next steps or a proposal for how the advocate would handle your matter, including how fees would work. Take time to read it and ask about anything that is unclear.

A first consultation does not commit you to instructing the advocate. Submitting an enquiry or attending a meeting does not by itself create an advocate–client relationship. That relationship usually begins once you and the advocate agree that they will act for you.

A calm, prepared start

Legal matters can feel overwhelming, but you do not have to have all the answers before you walk in. The point of a consultation is to help you understand your situation and make informed decisions.

title: Buying Land in Kenya: Due Diligence Before You Pay
excerpt: Land is one of the most valuable things many people will ever buy. Careful checks before any money changes hands help protect your investment.
content:
For many Kenyans, buying land is one of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make. It is also an area where mistakes can be costly and difficult to undo. Stories of buyers who paid for land that was not the seller's to sell, or that came with problems they did not know about, are sadly familiar.

The good news is that careful checks before you pay can significantly reduce those risks. This process is usually called due diligence. Here is a general overview of what it involves.

Start with an official search

The first step is usually an official search at the land registry. A search shows who is registered as the owner of the land and whether any interests, such as a charge to a bank, are recorded against the title. In some areas, searches and other land services are now carried out through the government's online land platform, while in others they are handled at the land registry. The process continues to change, so it is worth confirming the current procedure for the area where the land is located.

A search reflects the register at a point in time, so it is sensible to carry out an up-to-date search close to the time you commit to the purchase.

Verify the seller and their right to sell

Confirm that the person selling the land is the person shown on the register, or is properly authorised to sell on their behalf. Practical steps include:

  • Checking the seller's identification documents against the details on the title and search
  • Where the seller is a company, confirming that it exists and that the people dealing with you are authorised to act for it
  • Where the land belongs to someone who has died, confirming that the estate has been properly administered before any sale
  • Meeting the seller in person and being cautious of anyone who rushes the process

Check for encumbrances

An encumbrance is anything that limits the owner's ability to deal with the land. Common examples include charges in favour of lenders, cautions, caveats, restrictions and leases. Some may be cleared as part of the sale; others may make the purchase unwise until they are resolved. Your advocate can explain what any entries on the register mean and how they would need to be dealt with.

Look at the land itself

Documents tell only part of the story. Visit the land, preferably more than once, and speak to neighbours if you can. Check that the boundaries on the ground match the survey records and maps, that there is proper access, and that no one else is occupying or claiming the land. If anything seems inconsistent, pause and seek advice before going further.

If a deal feels rushed, or a seller resists reasonable checks, treat that as a reason to slow down rather than speed up.

Consents and approvals

Depending on the type of land and the circumstances, certain consents may be required before a sale can proceed. For example, transactions involving agricultural land may need the approval of the relevant land control board, and where land is matrimonial property, a spouse's consent may be required. Other approvals may apply to land in particular areas or held under particular types of title. An advocate can help you identify which apply to your purchase.

Use an advocate for the agreement and transfer

A well-drafted sale agreement sets out what is being sold, the price, how and when payment will be made, what each party must do and what happens if something goes wrong. It also gives you a clear record if any dispute arises later.

After the agreement comes the transfer. The transfer documents must be properly prepared, signed and registered under the Land Registration Act and the related land laws for ownership to pass to you. An advocate can manage this process, help ensure that payments are made safely and confirm that the land is registered in your name at the end.

Protect your investment

Every land transaction is different, and the right checks depend on the land, the seller and the type of title. What stays the same is the principle: verify before you pay.

title: Starting a Company in Kenya: What to Know Before You Register
excerpt: Registering a company is easier than it used to be, but the decisions you make at the start shape how your business runs. Here is what to think about first.
content:
Registering a business in Kenya has become more straightforward in recent years, with much of the process now handled online. But the ease of registration can hide how important the early decisions are. The structure you choose, the people you bring in and the records you keep will shape how your business operates for years to come.

Here is a general overview of what to think about before, and just after, you register. Requirements change from time to time, so always check the current position before you act.

Choose the right structure

Not every business needs to be a company. Common options in Kenya include:

  • Sole proprietorship: a business owned and run by one person, trading under a registered business name. It is simple to set up, but the owner is personally responsible for the business's debts.
  • Partnership: two or more people carrying on business together. A written partnership agreement is strongly advisable.
  • Limited liability partnership: a partnership structure that offers partners a degree of protection from the business's liabilities.
  • Private limited company: a separate legal entity, owned by shareholders and managed by directors, registered under the Companies Act. Owners' liability is generally limited.

The right choice depends on how many people are involved, the risks the business will take on, how you plan to raise money and how you want to be taxed. It is worth discussing these points before you register, because changing structure later can be more complicated.

Name search and registration

Business names and company registrations are handled by the Business Registration Service, largely through the government's online services platform. The usual first step is to search for and reserve a name. Choose a name that is distinctive and not too close to an existing business or brand, and remember that registering a name is not the same as protecting it as a trade mark.

Once the name is reserved, you submit the registration documents with details of the company, its directors and its shareholders. The process and the documents required are updated from time to time, so check the current requirements at the point you apply.

Directors and shareholders

Directors manage the company and owe it legal duties. Shareholders own it. In a small company the same people often play both roles, but the roles are different and so are the responsibilities.

When several people are involved, a shareholders' agreement can set out how decisions will be made, how shares can be transferred, what happens if someone wants to leave and how disagreements will be resolved. It is much easier to agree these points at the start than in the middle of a dispute.

The conversations that feel awkward at the start of a business are often the ones that prevent the hardest disputes later.

Tax registration

Every business has tax obligations. After registration, the company will need its own tax registration with the Kenya Revenue Authority, and depending on its activities it may need to register for particular taxes. Speak to a tax professional about which obligations apply to your business, and keep track of filing requirements from the outset.

Keeping records and staying compliant

Registration is the beginning, not the end. A company must keep certain registers and records, file returns and notify the registry of changes such as new directors or a change of registered office. Companies are also required to keep information about the people who ultimately own or control them. Licences or permits may also be needed, depending on what the business does and where it operates.

Good record-keeping from day one makes compliance easier, supports applications for finance and shows customers and partners that the business is run properly.

Getting it right from the start

Starting a business is exciting, and it is tempting to move quickly. Taking a little time to get the foundations right can save a great deal of trouble later.

title: Wills and Succession: Why Planning Ahead Protects Your Family
excerpt: Nobody likes to think about it, but a will is one of the most practical ways to protect the people you care about. Here is why planning ahead matters.
content:
Many people put off making a will. It can feel uncomfortable to think about, or like something to deal with later in life. Yet a will is one of the most practical ways to protect the people you care about, and making one is often simpler than people expect.

What a will does

A will is a written document that sets out how you want your property to be distributed after your death. It can also do much more than that. In a will, you can:

  • Decide who inherits your property, and in what shares
  • Appoint executors, the people you trust to manage your estate and carry out your wishes
  • Name guardians for young children
  • Make specific gifts, such as a particular piece of land or a family item
  • Set out wishes that help your family avoid misunderstandings later

In Kenya, wills and the administration of estates are governed mainly by the Law of Succession Act. For a will to be valid, it must meet certain formal requirements, including how it is signed and witnessed. A will that is not properly made may be challenged, which is one reason many people ask an advocate to help.

What happens without a will

When someone dies without a valid will, the law sets out how their estate is to be shared among their surviving family. The rules depend on who survives the person, for example a spouse, children or other relatives. The result may be quite different from what the person would have chosen.

Without a will, there is also no named executor. A family member will usually need to apply to court for a grant before they can deal with the estate. That process can take considerable time and effort, and it can be harder when family members disagree or when the deceased's affairs are unclear.

A will is not only about property. It is a way of giving your family clarity at a time when they will need it most.

Why planning ahead protects your family

Disputes over estates are, unfortunately, common. They can strain relationships and tie up property for long periods while matters are resolved. A clear, properly made will reduces the room for uncertainty and makes it easier for your executors to do their job.

Planning ahead also gives you an opportunity to think about practical questions. Who should look after your children? Is your property properly documented and registered? Do the people who will need to act know where to find important papers? Answering these questions now can save your family a great deal of difficulty later.

It is also worth knowing that the law allows certain dependants to apply to court for reasonable provision if they believe a will does not adequately provide for them. Good planning takes your family's circumstances into account from the start.

Keeping your will up to date

A will reflects your circumstances at the time you make it. Life changes, through marriage, children, separation, the purchase or sale of property, or the death of someone named in the will. It is sensible to review your will from time to time and whenever a significant change occurs.

Store your will safely and make sure your executors know where it is. A will that cannot be found cannot be followed.

When a loved one has died

If you are dealing with the estate of someone who has died, the process can feel overwhelming at an already difficult time. Generally, the first steps are to gather important documents, such as the death certificate and records of the person's property, and to find out whether they left a will. An advocate can then explain the process for applying for a grant and administering the estate.

Taking the first step

Making a will does not need to be complicated, but it does need to be done properly. If you would like to make or update a will, or need guidance on a succession matter, schedule a consultation or send us a message on WhatsApp. We will talk you through the process with care.
